title: Replace Words
directAnswer: Build a Trie from the dictionary of roots. For each word in the sentence, walk the trie character-by-character and stop at the FIRST node marked as a word-end — that's the shortest matching root, which is the replacement. If you fall off the trie (a missing child) or never hit a word-end, keep the original word. Building the trie is O(total root chars); replacing each word is O(its length), so the whole thing is O(total characters) — far better than testing every word against every root.

remember.pattern: Trie of roots + shortest-prefix lookup per word
remember.formula:
insert each root into a trie, mark isEnd on its last node

for each word in sentence:
    node = root; prefix = ""
    for ch in word:
        if ch not in node.children: break   # no root prefixes this word
        prefix += ch
        node = node.children[ch]
        if node.isEnd: replace with prefix; stop   # SHORTEST root wins
    else: keep the original word
rules: Stop at the **first isEnd** while walking — that yields the SHORTEST root, which the problem requires (`cat` beats `cattle`).
If a child is **missing mid-walk**, no root is a prefix → keep the **original word** unchanged.
If you finish the word **without hitting isEnd**, again keep the **original word** — a root must be a *prefix*, not a suffix or substring.
Build the trie **once** up front; then each sentence word is an independent O(L) lookup.
Track the matched prefix as you descend (or remember the depth) so you can emit it directly without re-slicing.
Roots replace words only as a **prefix from index 0** — never a match in the middle of the word.
whenToUse: You must match each query string against a SET of prefixes/roots efficiently
Many candidate prefixes share common beginnings (classic trie territory)
You need the SHORTEST (or longest) matching prefix, not just any membership
Dictionary is fixed and reused across many queries → amortize one trie build
antiSignals: Only one or two roots → a couple of `startsWith` checks beat building a trie
Matches can occur anywhere in the word, not as a leading prefix → this isn't a prefix problem
You need fuzzy / wildcard matching → that's a DFS-over-trie variant (Add and Search Words)
Roots don't share prefixes and the set is tiny → a HashSet of roots with length-bounded probing is simpler
remember.takeaway: Replace Words is the trie's bread-and-butter: index a set of roots so each word finds its shortest prefix in O(L). The 'stop at the first isEnd' tweak is the entire problem — it's the same children-map + isEnd skeleton as Implement Trie, just queried for the earliest word-end instead of the exact one. Once you see roots-as-a-trie, autocomplete and dictionary problems all collapse to this shape.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you reach for a trie to index many prefixes (instead of comparing every word against every root), and whether you correctly grab the SHORTEST root by stopping at the first word-end during the walk.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Comparing each sentence word against each root (O(words × roots × length) brute force), or matching the longest root instead of the shortest, or treating a missing child as a match and corrupting the output.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State that roots sharing prefixes scream 'trie', build it once, then explain that the first isEnd encountered during the descent is necessarily the shortest root — so a single early-terminating walk per word solves it in linear time.

problemStatement:
In English, we have a concept called **root**, which can be followed by some other word to form another longer word — let's call this word a **successor**. For example, when the root `"help"` is followed by the word `"ful"`, we can form a successor `"helpful"`.

Given a `dictionary` consisting of many roots and a `sentence` consisting of words separated by spaces, replace all the successors in the sentence with the **root forming it**. If a successor can be replaced by more than one root, replace it with the root that has the **shortest length**.

Return the sentence after the replacement.
constraints: dictionary[i] consists of only lowercase letters
sentence consists of only lowercase letters and spaces
The number of words in sentence is in the range [1, 1000]
Every two consecutive words in sentence are separated by exactly one space
understanding: For every word in the sentence, find the shortest dictionary root that is a PREFIX of it and swap the word for that root. If no root is a prefix, leave the word as-is. 'Shortest root wins' is the key rule, and 'prefix' means it must match from the very first character.

clarifyingQuestions.question: If multiple roots are prefixes of a word, which one do I use?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The shortest. If both "cat" and "cattle" are roots and the word is "cattle", the result is "cat". Stopping at the first word-end during the trie walk naturally gives the shortest.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Must the root be a leading prefix, or can it match anywhere?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: A leading prefix only — it must match starting at index 0. A root that appears in the middle of a word does not count.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What if no root is a prefix of a word?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Keep the original word unchanged. This happens when the walk hits a missing child or finishes the word without ever passing an isEnd node.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How large is the input, and does that affect the approach?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Up to 1000 roots and a sentence up to 10⁶ characters. Brute force (word × root comparisons) is too slow; a trie built once gives O(L) per word, which scales.

examples.input: dictionary = ["cat","bat","rat"], sentence = "the cattle was rattled by the battery"
examples.output: "the cat was rat by the bat"
examples.explanation: "cattle" → "cat", "rattled" → "rat", "battery" → "bat". "the", "was", "by" have no root prefix and stay unchanged.
Every word starts with a single-letter root, so each collapses to that letter.

examples.input: dictionary = ["catt","cat","bat","rat"], sentence = "the cattle was rattled by the battery"
examples.output: "the cat was rat by the bat"
examples.explanation: Both "catt" and "cat" prefix "cattle", but the shortest root "cat" wins — the walk hits cat's isEnd first.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: A trie indexes all roots by shared prefix; each word then finds its shortest root in one O(L) walk.

approaches.name: HashSet of Roots — Probe Each Prefix
approaches.whenToMention: A reasonable baseline that's clean for small dictionaries. Mention it to show the trade, then pivot to the trie when prefixes are shared and the dictionary is large.

complexity.time: O(total sentence chars × max root length)

hints: If you put every root in a hash set, how would you find the shortest root that prefixes a given word?
For each word, try its prefixes from shortest to longest: word[0:1], word[0:2], … and check each against the set. The first hit is the shortest root.
Cap the prefix length at the longest root so you don't probe forever; if no prefix is in the set, keep the original word.
approaches.complexityReasoning: For each word you build and hash up to L prefixes, and hashing a length-k prefix costs O(k); summed it's roughly O(L²) per word, or O(L × maxRootLen) if you cap at the longest root. Across the sentence that's O(total chars × maxRootLen). The set stores O(total root chars).
approaches.explanation:
Store all roots in a hash set, then for each sentence word generate its prefixes in increasing length and look each up. The first prefix found in the set is, by construction, the shortest root that prefixes the word.

**Why probe shortest-to-longest.** The problem wants the shortest matching root, so testing `word[0:1]`, then `word[0:2]`, and so on means the very first set hit is the answer — you stop immediately and never consider longer roots. Probing longest-first would force you to keep a running minimum and do more work.

**Why cap the prefix length.** A word can be far longer than any root, so probing every prefix up to the word's full length wastes time on prefixes that can't possibly be a root. Bounding the probe at the maximum root length keeps the inner loop tight.

**Why string slicing makes this quadratic-ish.** Each prefix `word[0:k]` is a fresh string of length `k` that must be built and hashed, so summing `k = 1..L` gives O(L²) work per word in the worst case. For a single 10⁶-character sentence split into ≤1000 words this is usually fine, but it's strictly more work than a trie, which reads each character once.

**Why it's still worth mentioning.** With only a handful of roots and no shared prefixes, this approach is shorter to write and has no node-allocation overhead. State it as the simple option, note its cost, then upgrade to the trie when the dictionary is large or prefix-heavy.
approaches.insight: The hash set can only answer 'is this exact string a root?', so you must manufacture every candidate prefix and test it. The trie flips that: it walks the word's characters once and the roots reveal themselves as isEnd nodes along the path — no prefix strings are ever materialized.

Not capping the prefix length at maxLen — wasted probes on impossibly long prefixes.
Using `roots.contains(word)` only (exact match) — misses the case where a shorter root prefixes the word.

approaches.name: Trie of Roots — Stop at First isEnd (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Frame it as 'index all roots in a trie, then each word walks the trie and the first word-end it passes is its shortest root'.

complexity.time: O(total root chars + total sentence chars)

hints: The roots share prefixes (cat, cattle, car all start with 'ca'). What structure stores shared prefixes once and lets you walk a word character-by-character?
Insert every root into a trie, marking isEnd on each root's final node. Then for each word, descend the trie one character at a time.

The moment you reach a node with isEnd = true, you've spelled out a complete root — and because you're walking from the start, it's the SHORTEST such root. Replace and stop. If a child is missing, keep the original word.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Building the trie inserts every root character exactly once → O(sum of root lengths). Replacing scans each sentence character at most once during its word's walk, with O(1) child lookups → O(sum of sentence lengths). No re-hashing of prefix substrings, so it strictly dominates the hash-set probing.
approaches.explanation:
Index the dictionary as a trie — a tree whose edges are characters and whose nodes flag where a root ends — then let each sentence word walk down it. The first `isEnd` node the walk passes spells the shortest root that prefixes the word.

**Why a trie is the right index.** Roots like `cat`, `cattle`, and `car` share the prefix `ca`. A trie stores that shared path once and branches only where the roots differ, so a single descent simultaneously checks the word against *all* roots that could prefix it. The hash set, by contrast, had to manufacture and test each candidate prefix separately.

**Why the first isEnd is the shortest root.** We descend from the root following the word's characters in order, so node depth equals prefix length. Word-ends appear in increasing depth as we go deeper. The instant we hit one, we've found a complete root, and since we've examined every shorter prefix already (and none was a word-end), this is by definition the shortest matching root. Stopping there is exactly the 'shortest root wins' rule — no comparison or min-tracking needed.

**Why a missing child means 'keep the word'.** If at some character the current node has no matching child, then no root continues along this path — and since we hadn't yet hit an isEnd, no root is a prefix of the word at all. We break out and emit the original word untouched. The same logic covers the case where we consume the whole word without ever passing an isEnd.

**Why building once pays off.** The trie is constructed a single time from the dictionary, then reused for every word in the sentence. With up to 1000 words against a 1000-root dictionary, amortizing the build across all queries is what turns a potential O(words × roots × length) brute force into linear time over the total input size.
approaches.insight: This is Implement Trie with one twist: instead of querying for an exact word (walk to the end, check isEnd) or a prefix's existence (walk, check the node exists), you query for the earliest word-end along the path. The children-map + isEnd skeleton is identical — only the stopping condition changes. Recognizing that 'shortest prefix in a set' = 'first isEnd on a trie walk' is the whole insight.

pitfalls: Continuing the walk past the first isEnd to find a longer root — the problem wants the shortest.
Creating child nodes during the query walk (copying insert logic) — corrupts the trie; the lookup must be read-only.
Returning an empty/garbage string when no root matches instead of the original word.

commonMistakes: Brute-forcing every word against every root — O(words × roots × length), too slow for the constraints.
Matching the longest root instead of the shortest by walking past the first isEnd.
Replacing the word even when no root is a prefix, instead of keeping the original.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Matching the longest root instead of the shortest
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If you keep descending after the first isEnd to find a deeper word-end, you return a longer root. The problem requires the shortest, so you must stop at the first isEnd.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Mutating the trie during lookup
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Reusing insert's 'create child if missing' inside the query walk silently inserts the query word as a root, so later words get wrongly replaced. The lookup must bail out, never create.

patternNote: Trie as a prefix index. Insert the roots once, then each word's shortest matching root is the first isEnd encountered on a single O(L) descent. Same children-map + isEnd skeleton as Implement Trie, queried for the earliest word-end. The trie-of-a-word-set idea powers Word Search II and autocomplete.
